source_text: Nunc interposito nomine idololatriae, quod solum subiectum sufficere debet ad abdicationem spectaculorum, alia iam ratione tractemus ex abundanti, propter eos maxime qui sibi blandiumtur quod non nominatim abstinentia ista praescripta sit. quasi parum etiam de spectaculis pronuntietur, cum concupiscentiae saeculi damnantur. nam sicut pecuniae uel dignitatis uel gulae uel libidinis uel gloriae, ita et uolupta tis concupiscentia est; species autem uoluptatis etiam spectacula . opinor, generaliter nominatae concupiscentiae continent in se et uoluptates, aeque generaliter intellectae uoluptates specialiter et in spectacula disseruntur.
thought_title: The general condemnation of desire covers shows
orientation: Tertullian has just argued that Christians abstain from idolatrous pleasures in their ears and eyes, and now turns to a further argument for those who claim no specific prohibition of shows exists.
pass_a_gloss: Now, with the name of idolatry interposed, which alone as a subject ought to suffice for the rejection of shows, let us treat by another reasoning from abundance, especially on account of those who flatter themselves that this abstinence has not been specifically prescribed. As if too little is pronounced even about shows, when the desires of the world are condemned. For just as of money or of rank or of gluttony or of lust or of glory, so also of pleasure there is desire; but the kinds of pleasure are also shows. I think, desires named generally contain in themselves also pleasures, and pleasures understood equally generally are discussed specially also in shows.

choices.why: Keeps the rhetorical idiom of arguing beyond what is necessary, matching the literal force of the Latin phrase.
The brief marks this phrase as the voice of those who claim no specific prohibition exists; the reflexive verb means self-deception, not mere hoping.
The glossary fixes concupiscentia as 'desire'; saeculi is rendered literally as 'of the world' to preserve the biblical resonance.
Preserves the genitive construction and the existential force of est, showing that pleasure is one object among many of desire.
rejected: there is a desire for pleasure

choices.english: but the kinds of pleasure are also shows
choices.why: Keeps the copula implied by the Latin and the word order, making shows a species of pleasure.
rejected: shows are also a kind of pleasure
the forms of pleasure include shows

pass_b_english: Now that I have brought in the name of idolatry, which alone should be enough as a ground for rejecting the shows, let me argue the matter from another angle, out of abundance. I do this especially for those who flatter themselves that this abstinence is not specifically prescribed. As if too little is pronounced against the shows when the desires of the world are condemned. For just as there is desire of money, of rank, of appetite, of lust, or of glory, so too there is desire of pleasure; and the kinds of pleasure are also shows. I think that desires, when named generally, contain pleasures within themselves; and pleasures, when understood equally generally, are discussed specifically in the shows as well.

polish.changed: I clarified the flow by breaking the opening sentence into two, making the target audience explicit, and smoothing the logical transitions so the argument reads naturally aloud without losing any of Tertullian's qualifications or claims.

notes.why: Multiple terms for the same concept of giving up shows; reader may think different things are meant.
notes.fix: Use 'renunciation of shows' consistently or note synonyms.
